Major medical

Major Medical Plans

*Sample for illustration only. Your actual plan details would be replaced here.

Major medical is the foundation of every great benefits package. It is comprehensive health insurance that protects your employees and their families, from everyday checkups to life's biggest surprises, and it is the first benefit job seekers look for.

Major medical plans typically cover:

  • Preventive careAnnual checkups, screenings and vaccines at no cost in network.
  • Doctor and specialist visitsPrimary care and specialist care, from routine visits to ongoing treatment.
  • Urgent careFast care for illnesses and injuries that can't wait but aren't emergencies.
  • Emergency room visitsCoverage for emergencies when every minute counts.
  • Hospital stays and surgeryInpatient care, outpatient procedures and surgery.
  • Lab work and imagingBlood work, X-rays and advanced imaging such as MRI and CT scans.
  • Maternity and newborn carePrenatal visits, delivery and care for the newest member of the family.
  • Mental health servicesCounseling, therapy and behavioral health support.
  • Prescription drugsCoverage for generic, brand-name and specialty medications.
  • Out-of-pocket maximumAn annual cap on what employees pay, so one serious illness or accident never has to become a financial crisis.

With Key HR, you can offer the same caliber of coverage as the largest employers, with plan options built to fit your team and your budget.

Prescriptions

Sample Prescription Drug List

All four sample UnitedHealthcare plans use the Essential 4-Tier Prescription Drug List (PDL). Every covered drug sits in a tier, and the tier sets the cost level at the pharmacy. Search the sample list below to see where common medications land.

TierCost LevelWhat's Included
Tier 1$ Lowest costMostly generic drugs, plus some brand names
Tier 2$$ Mid-rangeA mix of brand-name and generic drugs
Tier 3$$ Mid-rangeA mix of brand-name and generic drugs
Tier 4$$$ Highest costMostly brand-name drugs, plus some generics

Using a lower-tier drug can lower what you pay. Many Tier 4 drugs have lower-cost options in Tiers 1, 2 or 3, so ask your doctor if one could work for you.

Look up a medication (Sample)

Type a medication name or choose a category to search 1,978 drugs.

MedicationTierRequirements

Brand-name drugs are shown in UPPERCASE and generics in lowercase. This is the most commonly prescribed list, not every covered drug. If you don't see your medication, call the number on your UHC member ID card or check uhc.com.

Download the full lists (Sample)

The sample 2027 Prescription Drug List takes effect January 1, 2027.

What the requirement codes mean
H
Health care reform preventive. Generally covered at no cost to you.
H-PA
Preventive with prior authorization. May be covered at no cost if prior authorization criteria are met.
NF
Non-formulary. Not covered, but may be filled at the Tier 4 cost if certain criteria are met.
PA
Prior authorization. Your doctor must explain why you need the drug before the plan decides on coverage.
QL
Quantity limits. The most that is covered per copay or in a set period of time.
SP
Specialty medication. Treats complex or rare conditions and may need to come from a specialty pharmacy.
ST
Step therapy. You may need to try one or more other drugs first.

MEC plans cover only the services listed, including 100% preventive care, and meet the ACA minimum essential coverage requirement. They do not cover hospital stays, surgery or emergency room visits.

Minimum Value (RBP) pays providers up to 125% of the Medicare allowable amount; you may be billed for any balance above that. Inpatient, surgical and maternity services require precertification.

Monthly rates for the Minimum Value plans apply in all states except CA, CT and NY. Full benefits and plan notes are below.

MEC plan notes
  1. Costs include plan documents, MultiPlan network, ID cards, HealthWallet mobile application, enrollment guides, COBRA administration and claims management.
  2. Plans exclude out-of-network services and cover only the services listed above and on the Preventive Care Benefits page.
  3. Claims are repriced through the MultiPlan PHCS network. For services covered at a network discount, members will be responsible for paying the remaining balance after the network discount is applied. Discounts vary based on provider contracts.
  4. Prescription Drug Benefits are subject to the formulary. Copay amounts listed are based on a unit quantity of 30 for a 30-day supply. Pricing may vary based on quantity and supply.
  5. Virtual Health Benefits are offered through Recuro Health. Members have unlimited 24/7 access to virtual urgent care with board-certified doctors via phone, video or messaging. It also connects members with a Therapist or Licensed Counselor through secure and private online video or phone sessions at a $0 copay. Psychiatric services are available at an additional cost.

Exclusions & Using Your Plan

Notable exclusions

  • Abortion
  • Care outside the United States
  • Chemotherapy / radiation therapy
  • Cosmetic surgery
  • Dental care (mouth, jaws, teeth, oral surgery)
  • Dialysis
  • Durable medical equipment
  • Experimental / investigational treatments
  • Eye care and vision services
  • Hospice / private duty nursing
  • Infertility services / family planning
  • Nutritional supplements / vitamins
  • Self-injectable / GLP-1 drugs
  • Specialty drugs
  • Transplant services

This is a summary. Additional covered services, exclusions and limitations exist. Contact the plan administrator for full details.

Pharmacy

Prescriptions, at the counter or by mail

PureRx · ProCare PharmacyCare

At the pharmacy

Show your benefits card and ask the pharmacy to add your insurance profile. They will need the BIN, PCN, Member ID and Rx Group from your card. More than 60,000 retail pharmacies are in network.

Discounts

Save up to 80% on most eligible FDA-approved medications. On discount-only plans, you pay the remaining balance after the discount.

Member portal

Review pharmacy transactions at member.procarerx.com. PureRx member support: 888.899.5122.

Mail order and specialty

ProCare PharmacyCare ships at no charge in secure, confidential packaging. Have your doctor send prescriptions by ePrescribe (PPC-ProCare PharmacyCare, Miramar) or fax, then create your account at portal.procarerx.com.

FSA & HSA

Spending Accounts

Use pre-tax dollars to pay for health care, dependent care and commuting, and keep more of your paycheck.

Spending accounts

Pre-tax dollars, smarter spending.

FSA & HSA

Make every dollar go further. Set aside pre-tax money for medical, dental, vision and dependent care costs, and save roughly 25 cents on every dollar you spend.

Flexible Spending Accounts

Contribute what you expect to spend during the plan year; unused funds are generally forfeited.

Healthcare FSA

A Flexible Spending Account (FSA) lets you set aside money from your paycheck, before taxes, to pay for eligible health care expenses. You can use it to buy everyday items like pain relievers, allergy medicine, cold medicine, bandages, sunscreen, and other eligible over-the-counter (OTC) products. You do NOT have to enroll in your employer's medical insurance to participate in an FSA! You can have an FSA even if you have medical coverage somewhere else or no medical coverage at all. Remember, USE IT OR LOSE IT! Any money left in your account after the plan's deadline may be forfeited, so plan carefully when deciding how much to contribute.

Dependent Care FSA

Use your Dependent Care FSA funds to pay for eligible care expenses for children under age 13 or qualifying adult dependents who are unable to care for themselves. Eligible expenses may include daycare, before- and after-school care, summer day camps (overnight camps are not eligible), and adult daycare that allow you (and your spouse, if applicable) to work or look for work.

Also Available: Limited FSA, Commuter Parking & Transit Benefits

Commuter Benefits – Parking & Transit

Save money on your daily commute by using pre-tax dollars to pay for eligible parking and public transportation expenses. For 2027, you can set aside a projected $350 per month for parking and an additional $350 per month for transit, including buses, trains, and eligible vanpools. That's up to $700 per month in pre-tax savings opportunities, helping you reduce your taxable income and keep more of your paycheck!

A Paycheck Tale: Bob vs. Tom

Bob and Tom work side-by-side at the same company, each earning an annual salary of $52,000 ($2,000 gross per paycheck). Both men expect to spend about $1,300 a year ($50 per pay period) on predictable medical expenses like prescriptions, dental checkups, and new glasses.

During open enrollment, Bob enrolled in a Health FSA, while Tom decided not to enroll, thinking it was safer to just pay out of pocket.

Here is exactly how that single choice plays out over their 26 pay periods:

Pay Period vs. Annual FSA Comparison (26 Pay Periods)

FeaturePer Pay PeriodAnnual Total
Tom (No FSA)Bob (With FSA)Tom (No FSA)Bob (With FSA)
Gross Pay$2,000.00$2,000.00$52,000.00$52,000.00
Pre-tax FSA Deduction$0.00-$50.00$0.00-$1,300.00
Taxable Income$2,000.00$1,950.00$52,000.00$50,700.00
Estimated Taxes (30%)-$600.00-$585.00-$15,600.00-$15,210.00
Out-of-Pocket Medical Cost-$50.00$0.00-$1,300.00$0.00
Net Take-Home Pay$1,350.00$1,365.00$35,100.00$35,490.00
Total Annual Value Kept$35,100.00$35,490.00
Total Annual SavingsTom's Baseline+$390.00

How the Math Turns in Bob's Favor

  • The Tax Shield: Because Bob uses an FSA, the government only taxes him on $1,950 each pay period. Tom gets taxed on the full $2,000. Over the year, the IRS takes $15,600.00 from Tom, but only $15,210.00 from Bob.
  • The Bottom Line: Bob shields $1,300.00 of his hard-earned income from taxes. By doing this, he pays for his medical costs entirely tax-free, outperforming Tom's strategy and keeping an extra $390.00 cash in his pocket by the end of the year.
Health Savings Account

Tax-advantaged, yours for life.

When paired with a qualifying High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP), an HSA gives you triple tax advantages and a balance that stays with you year after year. HSA limits follow the calendar year. It is only available if you are enrolled in an HSA-qualified HDHP. See IRS Publication 502 for eligible expenses.

Why open an HSA?

Flexible options

Use funds tax-free for qualified medical, dental and vision care, now or in the future, even if your HSA-compatible coverage ends.

Tax advantages

Contributions are tax-deductible or pre-tax. Earnings grow tax-deferred. Qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

Long-term growth

HSA funds can be invested in stocks, bonds and mutual funds for greater earning potential (fees may apply).

Key features

  • No "use it or lose it"If you don't use it, save it for next year or for retirement. Your balance rolls over indefinitely.
  • Flexible contributionsContributions can come from you, your employer or third parties, up to your federal tax filing deadline.
  • You're in controlChoose when to use your HSA or pay out of pocket. You can fund it from existing HSAs, MSAs or IRAs.
  • Age 65 flexibilityAfter age 65, HSA funds can be used for non-qualified expenses with only income tax due and no penalty.

Supplemental coverage

Hospital Indemnity Insurance

Hospital indemnity insurance is a voluntary or employer-sponsored benefit that pays fixed cash benefits directly to employees when they have a qualifying hospital stay.

Unlike major medical, which pays doctors and hospitals based on negotiated rates and itemized bills, hospital indemnity pays your employee a set dollar amount for specific hospital events, no matter what their medical plan covers.

How it works

Simple, flexible cash when it is needed most

  • Cash paid directly to employeesBenefits go straight to the employee by check or direct deposit. The money can cover deductibles, copays and coinsurance, or everyday costs like rent, groceries, childcare and lost wages during recovery.
  • No network restrictionsHospital indemnity is not tied to a provider network, so the benefit is the same at any hospital, in or out of network.
  • Pays on top of other coverageBenefits are paid in addition to major medical, workers' compensation and other supplemental plans like accident or critical illness, with no reduction.
  • Simple claimsNo complex medical coding. Employees submit a claim form with their hospital admission and discharge paperwork and get paid quickly.

Why it matters

Why employers add hospital indemnity

The ideal partner for high-deductible plans

A hospital stay can leave employees on high-deductible plans facing thousands in out-of-pocket costs. Hospital indemnity helps bridge that gap for a modest payroll deduction, making higher-deductible medical plans an easier choice.

Valued by growing families

Many group plans waive waiting periods for pregnancy, so an employee who enrolls during open enrollment can receive a cash benefit when their baby arrives. It is one of the most appreciated voluntary benefits for growing families.

Guaranteed issue and portable

Group plans offered at hire or during open enrollment are typically guaranteed issue, with no medical exams or health questions. Most are portable, so employees can keep their coverage if they leave.

Benefits glossary

Glossary of Terms

A clear, practical guide to the plan types, costs and accounts you will see during open enrollment.

Plan Types & Network Models

HMO Health Maintenance Organization

A managed care plan where all non-emergency care must come from a defined local network of providers.

Network & referrals
You choose an in-network Primary Care Physician (PCP), and you need a PCP referral to see a specialist.
Out-of-network
Not covered, except for life-threatening emergencies.
Cost
Lowest premiums and lower copays, with the least provider flexibility.

PPO Preferred Provider Organization

A flexible plan with a broad network of preferred doctors and facilities, plus partial coverage for out-of-network care.

Network & referrals
No PCP required. You can see specialists directly without a referral.
Out-of-network
Covered, but with separate, higher deductibles and coinsurance.
Cost
Highest premiums in exchange for the most freedom to choose providers.

EPO Exclusive Provider Organization

Combines the direct specialist access of a PPO with the network limits of an HMO.

Network & referrals
No PCP or specialist referrals needed, but care is covered only at in-network providers.
Out-of-network
Not covered, except emergencies. You pay 100% for non-emergency out-of-network care.
Cost
Moderate premiums, lower than PPOs and similar to HMOs.

POS Point of Service

Combines HMO-style coordinated care with the option to go out of network like a PPO.

Network & referrals
You choose an in-network PCP and get PCP referrals for specialist visits.
Out-of-network
Covered. If your PCP refers you, the plan pays more. If you go on your own, coverage drops and you may need to file the claim yourself.
Cost
Moderate premiums with PCP-coordinated care.

HDHP High-Deductible Health Plan

A plan with a higher deductible and out-of-pocket maximum set by IRS rules, in exchange for lower premiums.

HSA compatible
A qualified HDHP is the only type of health plan you can pair with a Health Savings Account (HSA).
How you pay
Except for preventive care, which is covered at 100%, you pay the full contracted rate for care and prescriptions until you meet the deductible.
Cost
Lowest payroll deductions, with more cost up front when you use care.

Costs & How You Pay

Premium

The fixed amount paid each month to keep your coverage active, whether or not you use care. With employer plans, the cost is usually split between the employer and your pre-tax payroll deduction.

Deductible

The amount you pay each plan year for covered services before the plan starts paying.

Embedded
On a family plan, each person has their own deductible. Once one person meets it, the plan starts paying for them even if the family total is not met.
Aggregate
The full family deductible must be met before the plan pays coinsurance for anyone on the plan.

Copayment (Copay)

A flat dollar amount you pay at the time of service, for example $25 for primary care or $15 for a generic prescription. Copays are predictable, usually are not subject to the deductible on non-HDHP plans, and count toward your out-of-pocket maximum.

Coinsurance

Your percentage share of covered costs after you meet the deductible. On an 80/20 plan, the plan pays 80% of the allowed amount and you pay 20% until you reach your out-of-pocket maximum.

Out-of-Pocket Maximum

The most you will pay for covered in-network care in a plan year. Deductibles, copays and coinsurance all count toward it. Premiums, out-of-network balance bills and non-covered services do not. Once you reach it, the plan pays 100% of allowed in-network costs for the rest of the year.

Allowed Amount & Balance Billing

Allowed amount
The maximum payment the insurer and an in-network provider have agreed on for a service.
Balance billing
When an out-of-network provider bills you for the difference between their full charge and the allowed amount. The federal No Surprises Act prohibits this for emergency care and other care you could not choose.

Tax-Advantaged Healthcare Accounts

HSA Health Savings Account

Who owns it
You own it. It goes with you if you change jobs or retire.
Who can contribute
Employee and/or employer
Plan requirement
Must be enrolled in a qualified HDHP
Rollover rules
Funds roll over every year. No use-it-or-lose-it rule.

FSA Health Care Flexible Spending Account

Who owns it
Employer-owned. Stays with the company if you leave.
Who can contribute
Employee and/or employer
Plan requirement
Available with any plan, or no plan
Rollover rules
Use it or lose it, subject to a grace period or limited carryover.

Limited-Purpose FSA

Who owns it
Employer-owned. Stays with the company.
Who can contribute
Employee and/or employer
Plan requirement
Paired with an HDHP and HSA
Rollover rules
Limited carryover. Dental and vision expenses only.

Dependent Care FSA

Who owns it
Employer-owned. Stays with the company.
Who can contribute
Employee and/or employer
Plan requirement
Available with any health plan
Rollover rules
Use it or lose it. Covers qualifying child and elder day care.

HRA Health Reimbursement Arrangement

Who owns it
Employer-owned and 100% employer-funded.
Who can contribute
Employer only
Plan requirement
Set by the employer
Rollover rules
Set by the employer's plan document.

HSA Triple Tax Advantage

  • Contributions go in pre-tax or are tax-deductible.
  • Your balance grows tax-free through interest or investments.
  • Withdrawals are tax-free when spent on IRS-qualified medical expenses.
  • At age 65 and older, you can withdraw for non-medical expenses without penalty, paying only ordinary income tax.

Enrollment Rules & Protections

Qualifying Life Event (QLE)

A major life change that lets you change your benefits outside of open enrollment, also called a Special Enrollment Period.

Common events
Marriage, divorce, birth or adoption, death of a covered dependent, or losing other group coverage, such as when a spouse changes jobs.
Timeline
Changes generally must be made within 30 days of the event, or 60 days for loss of Medicaid or CHIP.

Section 125 / Cafeteria Plan

The IRS rule that lets your premiums, FSA and HSA contributions come out of your paycheck before federal income, Social Security and Medicare taxes. Because of this rule, once open enrollment closes your elections are locked in for the full plan year unless you have a qualifying life event.

Prior Authorization & Step Therapy

Prior authorization
Your provider must get the insurer's approval, showing medical necessity, before a procedure, surgery or specialty drug is covered.
Step therapy
You may need to try a lower-cost or generic drug first before the plan covers a higher-cost brand.

Formulary & Drug Tiers

The formulary is your plan's list of covered prescription drugs.

Tier 1
Generic. Lowest cost, with the same active ingredients as the brand name.
Tier 2
Preferred brand. Brand-name drugs on the plan's preferred list.
Tier 3
Non-preferred brand. Higher-cost brands when a generic or preferred option exists.
Tier 4
Specialty. High-cost biologics, injectables and complex therapies, often requiring prior authorization.

Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC)

A standard document required by the Affordable Care Act for every plan. It lists covered services, deductibles and copays, with sample cost scenarios such as having a baby, so you can compare plans side by side.

Voluntary & Supplemental Benefits

Short-Term Disability (STD)

Replaces part of your weekly income, typically 50% to 70%, after a short waiting period if a non-work illness, injury or recovery from childbirth keeps you from working.

Long-Term Disability (LTD)

Replaces part of your monthly income when a disability lasts beyond the short-term period, typically starting after 90 or 180 days, until you recover, reach retirement age or hit the benefit limit.

Critical Illness Insurance

Pays a lump-sum cash benefit directly to you when you are diagnosed with a covered illness such as cancer, heart attack or stroke, separate from your health plan.

Accident Insurance

Pays set cash amounts for accidental injuries and related care, such as ER visits, fractures, dislocations and concussions.

Hospital Indemnity

Pays a fixed cash benefit directly to you for each day you are admitted to the hospital, helping cover high deductibles.

EAP (Employee Assistance Program)

A free, confidential program offering short-term counseling, legal consultations and financial wellness support for you and your household.
